intro.why: Logistic and softmax regression are the output layers of almost every classifier network. The gradient ŷ − y, numerically stable softmax and mini-batch SGD introduced here are used unchanged in deep networks (Module 5) and Transformers (Module 9).
prereq: Linear regression as a neuron and gradient descent (Module 3)

symbols: weight matrix, column $\mathbf w_k$ per class
logits for one example / a batch

sections.title: What is classification?
sections.plain: Predict a discrete label.
sections.body: Definition (p.4): classification is a supervised learning task that predicts a discrete category or class label based on input features. Input $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^d$; output $y\in\{1,2,\dots,K\}$; goal: learn $f:\mathbb R^d\to\{1,\dots,K\}$ that assigns inputs to classes. Difference from regression: regression predicts continuous values (price, temperature); classification predicts discrete categories (spam/not spam, cat/dog).

sections.title: Examples of classification problems
sections.plain: Spam, diagnosis, images, sentiment.
sections.body:
• Email spam detection: input text, sender information, attachments; output spam or not spam.
  • Medical diagnosis: symptoms, test results, history; disease present or absent.
  • Image recognition: pixel values; object category (cat, dog, car…).
  • Sentiment analysis: review text; positive, negative or neutral (p.5).

sections.title: Types of classification
sections.plain: Binary, multi-class (exactly one of K), multi-label (any subset).
sections.body:
1. Binary: two classes, $y\in\{0,1\}$ or $\{-1,+1\}$; spam, disease diagnosis, fraud.
  2. Multi-class: $y\in\{1,\dots,K\}$, $K>2$; digits 0–9, animals; each example belongs to exactly one class.
  3. Multi-label: each example can belong to multiple classes simultaneously; movie genres (action + comedy), document tagging (p.6).

Output layers: binary → one sigmoid; multi-class → K-way softmax; multi-label → K independent sigmoids with binary cross-entropy each.

sections.title: Binary classification problem
sections.plain: Learn P(class 1 | x), threshold at 0.5.
sections.body: Definition (p.8): binary classification assigns each input to one of two classes. Notation: $y\in\{0,1\}$ with $y=1$ the positive class (spam, disease present) and $y=0$ negative; dataset $\mathcal D=\{(\mathbf x^{(i)},y^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^N$; goal: learn $f(\mathbf x)$ that outputs the probability of class 1. Decision boundary: predict $\hat y=1$ if $f(\mathbf x)\ge0.5$, else 0. The visual example (p.9) shows class-0 dots and class-1 crosses in $(x_1,x_2)$ separated by a straight decision boundary into Region 0 and Region 1: the boundary separates the two classes in feature space.

sections.title: Why not use linear regression?
sections.plain: Its outputs go below 0 and above 1.
sections.body: Problem (p.10): linear regression outputs $\hat y\in(-\infty,\infty)$, but we need probabilities $\hat y\in[0,1]$; a linear model can predict values $<0$ or $>1$ (the figure shows a line $y=wx+b$ through 0/1 data overshooting both). Solution: use a function that maps $(-\infty,\infty)\to[0,1]$. Squared error on 0/1 targets also penalises "too correct" predictions and is non-convex once composed with a sigmoid.

sections.title: What is logistic regression?
sections.plain: Linear score → sigmoid → probability.
sections.body:
Definition (p.12): logistic regression is a linear model for binary classification that uses the sigmoid function to output probabilities. Key idea: compute $z=\mathbf w^T\mathbf x+w_0$, apply $\hat y=\sigma(z)$, interpret $\hat y=P(y=1\mid\mathbf x)\in[0,1]$:

$$\hat y=\sigma(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\mathbf w^T\mathbf x}}\qquad(1)$$

Equivalently the log-odds are linear: $\log\frac{\hat y}{1-\hat y}=\mathbf w^T\mathbf x$.

sections.title: The sigmoid function and its properties
sections.body:
$$\sigma(z)=\frac1{1+e^{-z}},\qquad \sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))$$

Derivation of σ′: $\sigma'(z)=\frac{e^{-z}}{(1+e^{-z})^2}=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\cdot\frac{e^{-z}}{1+e^{-z}}=\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))$. At $z=0$: $\sigma(0)=0.5$, $\sigma'(0)=0.25$ (the maximum) (p.13).

Properties (p.14): range $(0,1)$, perfect for probabilities; monotonic (always increasing); smooth (differentiable everywhere); symmetry $\sigma(-z)=1-\sigma(z)$. Behaviour: $z\to+\infty$: $\sigma\to1$ (confident class 1); $z\to-\infty$: $\sigma\to0$ (confident class 0); $z=0$: 0.5 (uncertain). The derivative property makes sigmoid ideal for gradient-based learning. (p.13 shows the range as [0, 1] in places; strictly it's the open interval.)

sections.title: The four components for classification
sections.plain: Data, sigmoid neuron, cross-entropy, SGD.
sections.body:
1. Data: $d$-dimensional inputs and binary labels.
  2. Model: single neuron with sigmoid activation.
  3. Objective: binary cross-entropy loss.
  4. Learning algorithm: stochastic gradient descent (SGD).

Note (p.16): SGD is used instead of batch GD for efficiency (and for learning purposes).

sections.title: Matrix form of data
sections.plain: Same X as regression; labels are 0/1.
sections.body: Design matrix $X\in\mathbb R^{N\times(d+1)}$ with a leading column of ones, label vector $\mathbf y\in\{0,1\}^N$, weights $\mathbf w=[w_0,\dots,w_d]^T\in\mathbb R^{d+1}$. Key difference from regression: $y^{(i)}\in\{0,1\}$ is discrete, not continuous (p.17).

sections.title: Logistic regression as a single neuron; prediction
sections.plain: z = wᵀx, ŷ = σ(z) = P(y = 1 | x).
sections.body:
Inputs $1,x_1,\dots,x_d$ with weights $w_0,\dots,w_d$ → weighted sum $z$ → sigmoid → $\hat y$ (p.18).

$$z=\mathbf w^T\mathbf x=w_0+w_1x_1+\cdots+w_dx_d\ (2),\qquad \hat y=\sigma(z)=\frac1{1+e^{-z}}\ (3),\qquad \hat y=P(y=1\mid\mathbf x)\in[0,1]\ (4)$$

$z$ is the logit (pre-activation) and $\hat y$ the predicted probability (p.19).

sections.title: Making predictions: decision rule and boundary
sections.plain: Class 1 iff ŷ ≥ 0.5 iff wᵀx ≥ 0: a hyperplane.
sections.body:
$$\text{class}=\begin{cases}1&\hat y\ge0.5\\0&\hat y<0.5\end{cases}\ (5)\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \text{class}=\begin{cases}1&\mathbf w^T\mathbf x\ge0\\0&\mathbf w^T\mathbf x<0\end{cases}\ (6)$$

since $\sigma(z)=0.5$ when $z=0$. The decision boundary is $\mathbf w^T\mathbf x=0$, a hyperplane in feature space (p.20). Changing the 0.5 threshold trades precision against recall.

sections.title: Binary cross-entropy loss
sections.plain: −[y log ŷ + (1 − y) log(1 − ŷ)].
sections.body:
We cannot use squared error for classification; instead cross-entropy (p.21):

$$\ell(\mathbf w;\mathbf x^{(i)},y^{(i)})=-\Big[y^{(i)}\log\hat y^{(i)}+(1-y^{(i)})\log(1-\hat y^{(i)})\Big],\quad \hat y^{(i)}=\sigma(\mathbf w^T\mathbf x^{(i)})\qquad(7)$$

If $y=1$: loss $=-\log\hat y$ (penalises $\hat y$ far from 1); if $y=0$: $-\log(1-\hat y)$ (penalises $\hat y$ far from 0).

Derivation (MLE). Model $y\mid\mathbf x\sim\text{Bernoulli}(\hat y)$: $P(y\mid\mathbf x)=\hat y^{y}(1-\hat y)^{1-y}$. The negative log-likelihood of one example is exactly (7); for i.i.d. data the total NLL is the sum.

sections.title: Total loss function
sections.plain: Average BCE over the dataset; minimise it.
sections.body:
$$J(\mathbf w)=-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\Big[y^{(i)}\log\hat y^{(i)}+(1-y^{(i)})\log(1-\hat y^{(i)})\Big]\ (8),\qquad \mathbf w^*=\arg\min_{\mathbf w}J(\mathbf w)\ (9)$$

(p.22) There is no closed-form solution, so we use iterative optimisation. If the data are linearly separable, $J\to0$ only as $\|\mathbf w\|\to\infty$; regularisation or early stopping keeps the weights finite.

sections.title: Why cross-entropy?
sections.plain: MLE, punishes confident mistakes, convex, clean gradients.
sections.body:
Advantages (p.23): probabilistic interpretation (from maximum likelihood); appropriate for probabilities (heavily penalises confident wrong predictions); convex (single global minimum for logistic regression); well-behaved gradients with sigmoid. The plot shows $-\log\hat y$ (true class 1) rising steeply as $\hat y\to0$ and $-\log(1-\hat y)$ rising as $\hat y\to1$. Values (code ex1): $y=1$ with $\hat y=0.9$: 0.105; 0.5: 0.693; 0.1: 2.303; 0.01: 4.605. (The slide says the loss "increases exponentially"; it actually grows like $-\log$, unboundedly as the prediction approaches the wrong extreme.)

With squared error, $\partial\ell/\partial z=(\hat y-y)\hat y(1-\hat y)$, which vanishes when the neuron is saturated and confidently wrong; cross-entropy's $\hat y-y$ does not.

sections.title: From batch to stochastic gradient descent
sections.plain: Batch GD is slow per update; SGD uses one random example.
sections.body: Batch GD (from Module 3) uses all training examples per update: $ abla J(\mathbf w)= rac1N\sum_i abla\ell(\mathbf w;\mathbf x^{(i)},y^{(i)})$, $\mathbf w\leftarrow\mathbf w-\eta abla J$. Problems: slow for large datasets (all $N$ per update), high memory, redundant computation when examples are similar. Solution: SGD updates weights using one random example at a time: much faster iterations, lower memory (p.24).

sections.title: Stochastic gradient descent
sections.plain: Pick one example, compute its gradient, step.
sections.body: Key idea: instead of the full-dataset gradient, use the gradient of a single random example (p.25). At iteration $t$: (1) randomly select $(\mathbf x^{(i)},y^{(i)})$; (2) compute $ abla\ell(\mathbf w;\mathbf x^{(i)},y^{(i)})$ (a noisy but unbiased estimate: $\mathbb E_i[ abla\ell_i]= abla J$); (3) update $\mathbf w^{(t+1)}=\mathbf w^{(t)}-\eta abla\ell(\mathbf w^{(t)};\mathbf x^{(i)},y^{(i)})$. The noise in SGD helps escape poor local minima/saddles and often leads to better generalisation.

sections.title: Computing the gradient for SGD
sections.plain: ∇ℓ = (ŷ − y)x: error times input.
sections.body:
$$\nabla_{\mathbf w}\ell(\mathbf w;\mathbf x^{(i)},y^{(i)})=(\hat y^{(i)}-y^{(i)})\,\mathbf x^{(i)},\qquad \frac{\partial\ell}{\partial w_j}=(\hat y^{(i)}-y^{(i)})\,x_j^{(i)}\qquad(10)$$

for $j=0,\dots,d$ with $x_0^{(i)}=1$ for the bias (p.26). Remarkably simple: error $(\hat y-y)$ times direction $\mathbf x$, the same structure as the linear-regression gradient. (The slide writes $\nabla_{\mathbf w}\ell=\partial\ell/\partial w_j$, mixing vector and component notation.)

Derivation. $\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial\hat y}=-\frac y{\hat y}+\frac{1-y}{1-\hat y}=\frac{\hat y-y}{\hat y(1-\hat y)}$; $\frac{\partial\hat y}{\partial z}=\hat y(1-\hat y)$; $\frac{\partial z}{\partial w_j}=x_j$. Multiplying, the $\hat y(1-\hat y)$ terms cancel: $\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial w_j}=(\hat y-y)x_j$.

sections.title: SGD algorithm for logistic regression
sections.plain: Epochs; shuffle; per example: predict, gradient, update.
sections.body:
Algorithm 1: SGD for logistic regression (p.27)
Input:  D = {(x⁽ⁱ⁾, y⁽ⁱ⁾)}ᵢ₌₁..N, learning rate η, epochs T
Output: learned weights w
1  initialise w⁽⁰⁾ = 0 (or small random values)
2  for epoch = 1 to T do
3      shuffle D
4      for each example (x⁽ⁱ⁾, y⁽ⁱ⁾) in D do
5          ŷ⁽ⁱ⁾ = σ(wᵀx⁽ⁱ⁾)
6          ∇ℓ = (ŷ⁽ⁱ⁾ − y⁽ⁱ⁾) x⁽ⁱ⁾
7          w ← w − η ∇ℓ
8      optional: compute total loss J(w) for monitoring
9  return w

Complexity: $O(d)$ per update, $O(Nd)$ per epoch, $O(d)$ extra memory: the data can be streamed.

sections.title: SGD vs batch GD; benefits and challenges
sections.plain: Smooth but slow vs noisy but fast; mini-batches compromise.
sections.body:
Visual comparison (p.28): on loss contours around $\mathbf w^*$, batch GD takes a smooth, deterministic path; SGD a noisy, stochastic path but with much faster iterations.

Benefits (p.29): speed (one example per iteration); memory (datasets that don't fit in memory); online learning (update as new data arrives); generalisation (noise helps escape sharp minima); scalability. Challenges: noisy updates (path not smooth); more sensitive to η; may oscillate near the minimum (needs a decaying η to converge exactly); careful hyperparameter tuning. Common compromise: mini-batch SGD.

$$X=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&2\\1&3\\1&4\end{bmatrix},\quad \mathbf y=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\\1\\1\end{bmatrix},\quad \mathbf w=\begin{bmatrix}w_0\\w_1\end{bmatrix}\ (\text{p.31})$$

Hyperparameters $\eta=0.5$, $N=4$; $\mathbf w^{(0)}=[0,0]^T$; for all examples $z=0\Rightarrow\hat y=\sigma(0)=0.5$, so $\hat{\mathbf y}^{(0)}=[0.5,0.5,0.5,0.5]^T$ and $J=\log2=0.693$ (p.32).

sections.title: Numerical example: two SGD iterations and progress
sections.body:
Iteration 1 (p.33), example $(\mathbf x^{(1)},y^{(1)})=([1,1],0)$: $z=0$, $\hat y=0.5$; error $0.5-0=0.5$; $\nabla\ell=0.5\,[1,1]^T=[0.5,0.5]^T$; $\mathbf w^{(1)}=[0,0]^T-0.5[0.5,0.5]^T=[-0.25,-0.25]^T$.

Iteration 2 (p.34), example $([1,3],1)$: $z=[1\ 3][-0.25,-0.25]^T=-1.0$, $\hat y=\sigma(-1)=0.269$; error $0.269-1=-0.731$; $\nabla\ell=-0.731[1,3]^T=[-0.731,-2.193]^T$; $\mathbf w^{(2)}=[-0.25,-0.25]^T-0.5[-0.731,-2.193]^T=[0.116,0.847]^T$.

Progress (p.35): with $\mathbf w^{(2)}$, $\hat y^{(1..4)}=\sigma(0.963),\sigma(1.810),\sigma(2.657),\sigma(3.504)=0.724,0.859,0.934,0.971$ (all verified). The slide says examples 1 and 2 (label 0) are "moving toward 0", but they moved from 0.5 up to 0.724 and 0.859, i.e. away from 0; the mean loss actually rose from 0.693 to 0.836. Only examples 3 and 4 improved. This is normal for two noisy SGD steps; continuing for more epochs (code ex1) reaches $\mathbf w\approx(-15.1,6.1)$, loss 0.024, with the decision boundary at 2.47 hours.

sections.title: Computational graph for one SGD step
sections.plain: w, x → z → σ → ŷ → error → loss; gradient back to w.
sections.body: (p.36) Weights $\mathbf w^{(t)}$ and input $\mathbf x^{(i)}$ meet at a multiply node → $z$ → $\sigma$ → $\hat y$; subtracting the label gives the error $e$ → loss $\ell$. Backward: $e$ times $\mathbf x$ gives $\nabla\ell$, scaled by $-\eta$ to produce $\mathbf w^{(t+1)}$. A single example per iteration: much faster than batch GD.

sections.title: Evaluating classification models
sections.plain: Accuracy, error types, positive-class performance; train/val/test.
sections.body: Unlike regression, we need different metrics (p.38). Key questions: how often is the model correct (accuracy)? what types of errors (confusion matrix)? how well does it identify positive cases (precision, recall)? Data split: training set (learn $\mathbf w$, typically 90–99%), validation set (tune hyperparameters, typically 10–15%), test set (final evaluation, typically 1–10%). Always evaluate on unseen test data. (The quoted percentages don't add up to 100% as ranges; they reflect large-data practice.)

sections.title: Confusion matrix
sections.plain: TP, FN / FP, TN; FP = type I, FN = type II.
sections.body:
Predicted positive (1)Predicted negative (0)
Actual positive (1)True positive (TP)False negative (FN)
Actual negative (0)False positive (FP)True negative (TN)

TP: correctly predicted positive; TN: correctly predicted negative; FP: incorrectly predicted positive (type I error); FN: incorrectly predicted negative (type II error) (p.39).

sections.title: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and when to use them
sections.plain: Correct overall; correct among predicted +; found among actual +; harmonic mean.
sections.body:
$$\text{Accuracy}=\frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN}\ (11),\qquad \text{Precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP}\ (12),\qquad \text{Recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}\ (13),\qquad F1=2\cdot\frac{\text{Precision}\times\text{Recall}}{\text{Precision}+\text{Recall}}\ (14)$$

(p.40–41) Precision: of predicted positives, how many are correct; recall (sensitivity): of actual positives, how many did we find; F1: their harmonic mean.

When to use (p.42): accuracy when classes are balanced; misleading with imbalanced data (e.g. 95% negative: always predicting negative scores 95%). Precision when false positives are costly (spam: don't mark real emails as spam). Recall when false negatives are costly (disease detection: don't miss sick patients). F1 when you need a balance; good for imbalanced datasets.

sections.title: Summary: binary classification
sections.plain: Data → sigmoid neuron → cross-entropy → SGD.
sections.body:
Cycle (p.44): (1) data $\{(\mathbf x^{(i)},y^{(i)})\}$, $y\in\{0,1\}$, shuffled each epoch → sample → (2) model: Σ, σ, sigmoid output → predict → (3) loss: cross-entropy $-[y\log\hat y+(1-y)\log(1-\hat y)]$ → gradient → (4) SGD: one example per update $\mathbf w^t\to\mathbf w^{t+1}$ → next. This framework is the foundation for neural networks.

Key takeaways (p.45): binary classification predicts $y\in\{0,1\}$; sigmoid maps to probabilities; logistic regression = linear model + sigmoid; cross-entropy is the appropriate objective; SGD updates one example at a time (faster, more scalable); feature scaling is essential for convergence and numerical stability; evaluation metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, confusion matrix; the framework extends to multi-class and deep networks.

sections.title: Multi-class classification: definition and examples
sections.plain: Exactly one of K > 2 classes; output a distribution.
sections.body:
Definition (p.47): assign each input to one of $K$ classes, $K>2$. Classes $y\in\{1,\dots,K\}$ (or $\{0,\dots,K-1\}$); each example belongs to exactly one class; output a probability distribution over all $K$ classes with $\sum_kP(y=k\mid\mathbf x)=1$. Example: a handwritten digit → probabilities for 0–9 → predict the class with highest probability.

Examples (p.48): MNIST (28×28 image → one of 10 digits); ImageNet (colour image → one of 1000 categories); text classification (news article → politics, sports, technology, entertainment, business); speech recognition (audio features → phoneme class). Visual (p.49): three clusters with decision boundaries separating $K=3$ classes; key insight: we need multiple output neurons (one per class) and a way to convert their outputs into a valid probability distribution.

sections.title: Four components for multi-class
sections.plain: K linear outputs + softmax + categorical CE + mini-batch SGD.
sections.body:
1. Data: features and labels $y\in\{1,\dots,K\}$.
  2. Model: linear model with $K$ output neurons (no hidden layers).
  3. Activation: softmax to produce a probability distribution.
  4. Objective: categorical cross-entropy.
  5. Learning algorithm: mini-batch stochastic gradient descent.

We now use mini-batch SGD instead of single-example SGD for better efficiency and stability (p.51).

sections.title: Data representation and one-hot encoding
sections.plain: Integer labels vs one-hot vectors of length K.
sections.body:
Inputs $X\in\mathbb R^{N\times(d+1)}$ as before. Class labels have two representations (p.52): integer encoding $\mathbf y\in\{1,\dots,K\}^N$, e.g. $\mathbf y=[3,1,2,1,3]^T$; one-hot encoding $Y\in\{0,1\}^{N\times K}$ (preferred for computation).

One-hot (p.53): class $k$ → a length-$K$ vector of zeros with a 1 at position $k$; for $K=4$: class 1 = $[1,0,0,0]^T$, class 2 = $[0,1,0,0]^T$, class 3 = $[0,0,1,0]^T$, class 4 = $[0,0,0,1]^T$. Why: treats all classes equally (no implicit ordering), matches the format of softmax outputs, simplifies loss computation, standard in DL frameworks (which often accept integer labels and one-hot internally).

sections.title: Weight matrix for multi-class
sections.plain: W is (d + 1) × K: one column per class.
sections.body:
$$W=\begin{bmatrix}w_{0,1}&w_{0,2}&\cdots&w_{0,K}\\w_{1,1}&w_{1,2}&\cdots&w_{1,K}\\\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\w_{d,1}&w_{d,2}&\cdots&w_{d,K}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{(d+1)\times K}$$

Each column $\mathbf w_k$ holds the weights for class $k$ (each class has its own linear model); row 0 holds the bias terms; total parameters $(d+1)\times K$, versus one weight vector for binary (p.54). For MNIST (784 pixels, 10 classes): $785\times10=7{,}850$ parameters.

sections.title: Architecture and logits
sections.plain: z = Wᵀx (K logits), Z = XW for a batch.
sections.body:
Architecture (p.55): inputs $1,x_1,\dots,x_d$ fully connected to logits $z_1,\dots,z_K$, then a softmax block giving $\hat y_1,\dots,\hat y_K$: $\mathbf z=W^T\mathbf x$ (linear) → $\hat{\mathbf y}=\mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf z)$ (activation).

$$\mathbf z=W^T\mathbf x=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf w_1^T\mathbf x\\\vdots\\\mathbf w_K^T\mathbf x\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}z_1\\\vdots\\z_K\end{bmatrix}\ (15),\quad z_k=w_{0,k}+w_{1,k}x_1+\cdots+w_{d,k}x_d;\qquad Z=XW\in\mathbb R^{N\times K}\ (16)$$

Each row of $Z$ contains one example's logits. Logits are unbounded in $(-\infty,\infty)$: not probabilities yet (p.56).

sections.title: The softmax function and its properties
sections.plain: Exponentiate and normalise: a probability distribution that keeps order.
sections.body:
$$\mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf z)_k=\frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^Ke^{z_j}}\ (17),\qquad \hat y_k=P(y=k\mid\mathbf x)=\frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_je^{z_j}}\ (18)$$

Purpose: convert $K$ logits into a valid probability distribution; $\hat y_k$ is the predicted probability for class $k$ (p.57). Properties (p.58): (1) $\hat y_k\in(0,1)$; (2) $\sum_k\hat y_k=1$; (3) preserves order ($z_i>z_j\Rightarrow\hat y_i>\hat y_j$); (4) translation invariant: $\mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf z)=\mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf z+c)$; (5) differentiable; (6) reduces to sigmoid for $K=2$. The exponential amplifies differences: larger logits get much larger probabilities.

Proofs. (4): $\frac{e^{z_k+c}}{\sum_je^{z_j+c}}=\frac{e^ce^{z_k}}{e^c\sum_je^{z_j}}$. (6): with $K=2$, $\hat y_1=\frac{e^{z_1}}{e^{z_1}+e^{z_2}}=\frac1{1+e^{-(z_1-z_2)}}=\sigma(z_1-z_2)$. Jacobian: $\frac{\partial\hat y_k}{\partial z_j}=\hat y_k(\delta_{kj}-\hat y_j)$.

sections.title: Softmax: numerical example
sections.body: Logits $\mathbf z=[2.0,1.0,0.1]^T$, $K=3$ (p.59). Step 1: $e^{2.0}\approx7.39$, $e^{1.0}\approx2.72$, $e^{0.1}\approx1.11$. Step 2: sum $=11.22$. Step 3: $\hat y_1=7.39/11.22\approx0.659$, $\hat y_2\approx0.242$, $\hat y_3\approx0.099$. Step 4: $\arg\max_k\hat y_k=1$ (verified, code ex2).

sections.title: Complete forward pass
sections.plain: Z = XW, Ŷ = softmax row-wise, k̂ = argmax.
sections.body:
$$Z=XW\in\mathbb R^{N\times K}\ (19),\qquad \hat Y=\mathrm{softmax}(Z)\in[0,1]^{N\times K}\ (20),\qquad \hat k=\arg\max_k\hat y_k\ (21)$$

Softmax is applied row-wise (to each example); each row of $\hat Y$ is a probability distribution over $K$ classes (p.60). Cost $O(NdK)$.

sections.title: Categorical cross-entropy
sections.plain: −Σ y_k log ŷ_k = −log(probability of the true class).
sections.body:
$$J(W)=-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{k=1}^Ky_k^{(i)}\log\hat y_k^{(i)}\qquad(22)$$

Goal: minimise $J(W)$ to find $W^*$ (p.61). Intuition (p.62): the loss depends only on the predicted probability of the true class; heavily penalises confident wrong predictions; encourages high probability for the correct class. Example, true class 2 ($\mathbf y=[0,1,0]$):

Prediction$\hat y_1$$\hat y_2$Loss $=-\log\hat y_2$
Good0.10.80.22
Medium0.30.50.69
Bad0.70.21.61
Very bad0.90.053.00

(Verified. The slide again says "exponentially"; the growth is logarithmic in $1/\hat y$.) Why (p.63): probabilistic (MLE of a categorical distribution), naturally handles $K$ classes, works well with softmax (numerically stable gradient), penalises wrong confidence, convex for linear models. Connection to binary: for $K=2$, $-[y_1\log\hat y_1+y_2\log\hat y_2]$ equals $-[y\log\hat y+(1-y)\log(1-\hat y)]$ with $y_2=y$, $y_1=1-y$.

sections.title: From SGD to mini-batch SGD; key concepts
sections.plain: B examples per update; ⌈N/B⌉ iterations per epoch.
sections.body:
Recap (p.65): batch GD uses all $N$ per update (slow but stable, accurate gradient); SGD uses 1 (fast but noisy, unstable); mini-batch SGD uses a small batch of $B$ examples ($1

Why (p.66): computational efficiency (vectorised matrix operations, better GPU utilisation); gradient estimation (less noisy than single-example SGD, more stable convergence; the variance falls as $1/B$); generalisation (noise helps escape sharp minima, often better test performance); memory efficiency (datasets larger than memory, loaded in batches).

Key concepts (p.67): batch size $B$ (small 32–64: more noise, faster iterations; medium 128–256: balanced; large 512–1024: less noise, slower convergence per epoch); iteration = one weight update (one mini-batch); epoch = one pass through the dataset.

$$\text{Iterations per epoch}=\lceil N/B\rceil\qquad(23)$$

Example: $N=60{,}000$, $B=128$: $\lceil60000/128\rceil=469$ iterations per epoch; after 10 epochs, $4{,}690$ weight updates.

sections.title: Mini-batch gradient and update rule
sections.plain: ∇J_B = (1/B) X_Bᵀ(Ŷ_B − Y_B).
sections.body:
$$ abla J_{\mathcal B}(W)= rac1B\sum_{i\in\mathcal B} abla\ell(W;\mathbf x^{(i)},\mathbf y^{(i)})\ (24),\qquad abla_WJ_{\mathcal B}= rac1BX_{\mathcal B}^T(\hat Y_{\mathcal B}-Y_{\mathcal B})\ (25)$$

with $X_{\mathcal B}\in\mathbb R^{B imes(d+1)}$ mini-batch inputs, $\hat Y_{\mathcal B}\in\mathbb R^{B imes K}$ predicted probabilities, $Y_{\mathcal B}\in\mathbb R^{B imes K}$ one-hot labels (p.68). Update (p.69):

$$W^{(t+1)}=W^{(t)}-\eta abla J_{\mathcal B}(W^{(t)})\ (26),\qquad W^{(t+1)}=W^{(t)}- rac{\eta}{B}X_{\mathcal B}^T(\hat Y_{\mathcal B}-Y_{\mathcal B})\ (27)$$

Derivation of (25). For one example, $\ell=-\sum_ky_k\log\hat y_k$. Using the softmax Jacobian, $ rac{\partial\ell}{\partial z_j}=-\sum_ky_k(\delta_{kj}-\hat y_j)=\hat y_j\sum_ky_k-y_j=\hat y_j-y_j$ (since $\sum_ky_k=1$). With $z_j=\mathbf w_j^T\mathbf x$, $ rac{\partial\ell}{\partial W}=\mathbf x(\hat{\mathbf y}-\mathbf y)^T$; averaging over the batch and stacking rows gives (25). Same "input × error" form as binary logistic and linear regression.

sections.title: Mini-batch SGD algorithm
sections.plain: Shuffle; per batch: logits, softmax, gradient, update.
sections.body:
Algorithm 2: mini-batch SGD for multi-class classification (p.70)
Input:  D = {(x⁽ⁱ⁾, y⁽ⁱ⁾)}, batch size B, learning rate η, epochs T
Output: learned weight matrix W
1  initialise W ~ N(0, 0.01)              # small random values
2  for epoch = 1 to T do
3      shuffle D
4      for each mini-batch 𝓑 of size B do
5          Z_𝓑 = X_𝓑 W                     # logits          O(BdK)
6          Ŷ_𝓑 = softmax(Z_𝓑)              # row-wise
7          ∇J = (1/B) X_𝓑ᵀ(Ŷ_𝓑 − Y_𝓑)      # gradient        O(BdK)
8          W ← W − η ∇J
9      optional: compute total loss for monitoring
10 return W

Cost per epoch $O(NdK)$; memory $O(BdK)$ beyond $W$. ($\mathcal N(0,0.01)$: 0.01 is usually the variance or standard deviation; frameworks differ.)

sections.title: Choosing the batch size
sections.plain: Small = noisy & fast; large = stable but memory-hungry; start at 128–256.
sections.body:
Batch sizeAdvantagesDisadvantages
Small (32–64)Fast iterations; more updates per epoch; better generalisation; escapes sharp minimaNoisy gradients; unstable training; poor GPU utilisation
Medium (128–256)Good balance; stable training; good GPU usage; standard choiceMay need tuning
Large (512–1024)Stable gradients; better GPU utilisation; faster per-epoch timeSlow convergence (fewer updates); may generalise worse; more memory

Rule of thumb: start with $B=128$ or $256$ (p.71). When changing $B$, scale η roughly proportionally (linear scaling rule) with warmup (Module 10).

sections.title: Numerical example: one mini-batch step
sections.plain: 4 points, 3 classes, B = 2, η = 0.1.
sections.body:
Setup (p.73–74): 4 points $(x_1,x_2,\text{class})$ = (1,2,1), (2,1,2), (2,3,1), (3,2,3); $K=3$, $d=2$, $N=4$, $B=2$, $\eta=0.1$.

$$X=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&2\\1&2&1\\1&2&3\\1&3&2\end{bmatrix},\quad Y=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix},\quad W^{(0)}=\begin{bmatrix}0.1&-0.1&0.2\\0.2&0.1&-0.1\\-0.1&0.2&0.1\end{bmatrix}$$

Step 1, logits (p.75) for the first two examples: $Z_{\mathcal B}=X_{\mathcal B}W^{(0)}$. Row 1 $=(0.1,0.4,0.3)$ ✓. Row 2 $=[1,2,1]W^{(0)}=(0.1+0.4-0.1,\ -0.1+0.2+0.2,\ 0.2-0.2+0.1)=(0.4,0.3,0.1)$; the slide prints $(0.4,0.2,0.1)$.

Step 2, softmax (p.76): $\hat{\mathbf y}^{(1)}=(0.280,0.378,0.342)$ ✓. For example 2 the correct value is $\mathrm{softmax}(0.4,0.3,0.1)=(0.378,0.342,0.280)$; the slide's $(0.387,0.315,0.298)$ matches neither its own logits nor the correct ones.

Step 3, gradient (p.77): $\nabla J=\frac12X_{\mathcal B}^T(\hat Y_{\mathcal B}-Y_{\mathcal B})$. Recomputed: $\begin{bmatrix}-0.171&-0.140&0.311\\0.018&-0.469&0.451\\-0.531&0.049&0.482\end{bmatrix}$ (slide: $\begin{bmatrix}-0.167&-0.154&0.320\\-0.024&-0.496&0.469\\-0.527&0.036&0.491\end{bmatrix}$, inheriting the softmax error).

Step 4, update (p.78): $W^{(1)}=W^{(0)}-0.1\nabla J=\begin{bmatrix}0.117&-0.086&0.169\\0.198&0.147&-0.145\\-0.047&0.195&0.052\end{bmatrix}$ (slide $\begin{bmatrix}0.117&-0.085&0.168\\0.202&0.150&-0.147\\-0.047&0.196&0.051\end{bmatrix}$: close, because η is small). The mini-batch loss falls from 1.173 to 1.071. Then process the next mini-batch (examples 3–4) and continue for multiple epochs; after 100 epochs all four points are classified correctly (code ex2).

sections.title: Computational graph for a mini-batch
sections.plain: W, X_B → Z_B → softmax → Ŷ_B; minus Y_B → E → J.
sections.body: (p.79) $W$ and the batch $X_{\mathcal B}$ multiply to $Z_{\mathcal B}$ → softmax → $\hat Y_{\mathcal B}$; subtracting labels $Y_{\mathcal B}$ gives $E$ → loss $J$. Backward: $\frac1BX_{\mathcal B}^TE$ gives $\nabla J$, scaled by $-\eta$ to give $W^{new}$. Mini-batch processes $B$ examples simultaneously: efficient and stable.

sections.title: Inference: making predictions
sections.plain: Logits → softmax → argmax; report the probabilities as confidence.
sections.body:
$$\mathbf z=W^T\mathbf x_{new}\ (28),\qquad \hat{\mathbf y}=\mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf z)\ (29),\qquad \hat k=\arg\max_{k=1..K}\hat y_k\ (30)$$

Optionally report confidence scores (the probabilities) (p.81). Example (p.82): $K=3$, $\mathbf x=[1,2.5,1.8]^T$, logits $\mathbf z=[1.2,2.5,0.8]^T$; $e^{1.2}\approx3.32$, $e^{2.5}\approx12.18$, $e^{0.8}\approx2.23$, sum 17.73; $\hat{\mathbf y}=[0.187,0.687,0.126]^T$; $\hat k=2$ with 68.7% confidence (verified). Softmax "confidence" is not automatically calibrated; temperature scaling can fix that. For prediction alone, argmax of the logits suffices (softmax preserves order).

sections.title: Multi-class accuracy and confusion matrix
sections.plain: Accuracy = trace / N; K × K matrix, rows actual, columns predicted.
sections.body:
$$\text{Accuracy}=\frac{\text{correct predictions}}{N}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb 1[\hat y^{(i)}=y^{(i)}]\qquad(31)$$

Confusion matrix (p.84): $K\times K$; row $i$, column $j$ = number of class-$i$ examples predicted as class $j$; diagonal correct, off-diagonal misclassifications. Per-class precision and recall are computed one-vs-all and averaged (macro or weighted).

Example (p.85): rows (45, 3, 2), (5, 38, 7), (2, 4, 44); row sums 50 each; accuracy $(45+38+44)/150=0.847$. Per-class (code ex2): precision (0.865, 0.844, 0.830), recall (0.90, 0.76, 0.88), F1 (0.882, 0.800, 0.854); class 2 is most often confused with class 3.

sections.title: Per-class metrics and averaging strategies
sections.plain: Precision_k, Recall_k, F1_k; macro = plain mean, weighted = by class frequency.
sections.body:
$$\text{Precision}_k=\frac{TP_k}{TP_k+FP_k}\ (32),\qquad \text{Recall}_k=\frac{TP_k}{TP_k+FN_k}\ (33),\qquad F1_k=2\cdot\frac{\text{Precision}_k\times\text{Recall}_k}{\text{Precision}_k+\text{Recall}_k}\ (34)$$

(p.86) Precision for class $k$: of all predictions for class $k$, what fraction were correct; recall: of all actual class-$k$ examples, what fraction we identified.

$$\text{Precision}_{macro}=\frac1K\sum_{k=1}^K\text{Precision}_k\ (35),\qquad \text{Precision}_{weighted}=\sum_{k=1}^Kw_k\cdot\text{Precision}_k,\ w_k=N_k/N\ (36)$$

Macro treats all classes equally (good when classes are equally important); weighted accounts for class imbalance (good when some classes are more common) (p.87). A third option, micro-averaging, pools counts across classes and equals accuracy for single-label problems.

sections.title: Top-k accuracy
sections.plain: Correct if the true class is among the k highest scores.
sections.body:
$$\text{Top-}k\text{ Accuracy}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb 1\big[y^{(i)}\in\text{Top-}k(\hat{\mathbf y}^{(i)})\big]\qquad(37)$$

For problems with many classes (ImageNet, 1000): top-1 asks whether the highest-probability class is correct; top-5 whether the true class is among the top 5 predictions. More forgiving for large $K$; captures whether the model has the right class among the top candidates; standard in the ImageNet challenge (p.88). Random guessing gives top-$k$ ≈ $k/K$.

sections.title: Summary: multi-class classification
sections.plain: Data → K neurons + softmax → categorical CE → mini-batch SGD.
sections.body: (p.89) (1) Data $X\in\mathbb R^{N\times(d+1)}$, $Y\in\{0,1\}^{N\times K}$ (one-hot), $W\in\mathbb R^{(d+1)\times K}$ → batch → (2) model: $K$ neurons + softmax → predict → (3) loss: cross-entropy $-\sum_ky_k\log\hat y_k$ → gradient → (4) mini-batch SGD with batch size $B$, $\nabla J_{\mathcal B}$, $W^t\to W^{t+1}$ → iterate.

sections.title: Implementation tips
sections.plain: η ∈ {0.01, 0.1, 1}, small random init, B ∈ {64, 128, 256}, shuffle, standardise, stable softmax.
sections.body:
1. Learning rate and epochs: start $\eta\in\{0.01,0.1,1.0\}$; typically 10–100 epochs; use early stopping.
  2. Weight initialisation: $w_j\sim\mathcal N(0,0.01)$; avoid zeros or large values. (For a single softmax layer zeros are actually fine; symmetry is only a problem with hidden layers.)
  3. Batch size: start $B\in\{64,128,256\}$; powers of 2 preferred; larger is stable but slower, smaller noisy but faster.
  4. Data handling: always shuffle each epoch; check class balance.
  5. Feature scaling (essential): standardisation $x'_j=(x_j-\mu_j)/\sigma_j$ prevents sigmoid saturation.
  6. Numerical stability: use $\log(\sigma(z))$ directly; stable softmax with $c=\max_kz_k$: $\mathrm{SM}(z)_k=\frac{e^{z_k-c}}{\sum_je^{z_j-c}}$; log-sum-exp trick prevents overflow/underflow (p.91).

The log-sum-exp identity: $\log\sum_je^{z_j}=c+\log\sum_je^{z_j-c}$, so $\log\hat y_k=z_k-c-\log\sum_je^{z_j-c}$; frameworks fuse softmax and cross-entropy (e.g. nn.CrossEntropyLoss takes raw logits).

sections.title: Debugging checklist
sections.plain: NaN, same class, oscillation, softmax ≠ 1, no progress, overfitting; sanity checks.
sections.body:
SymptomChecks / fixes (p.92)
Loss is NaN/Infη too large → decrease; check log(0) in the loss; scale features; use stable softmax
Predicts the same classCheck class balance; verify softmax/loss; η might be too small; verify one-hot encoding
Loss oscillatesη too large; use mini-batches; apply learning-rate decay
Softmax outputs don't sum to 1Implementation bug; numerical precision; use stable softmax
Loss not decreasingCheck gradient signs; η too small/large; verify feature scaling; verify data shuffling; check one-hot encoding
High train, low test accuracyOverfitting: add regularisation, get more data, simpler model
Sanity checksTiny dataset → 100% accuracy; verify $\hat y\in[0,1]$; verify $\sum_k\hat y_k=1$; shuffling improves results; print the confusion matrix

Recaps (p.98–99): logistic regression: sigmoid maps a linear combination to a probability, optimised by minimising cross-entropy, trained with SGD. Multi-class: multiple outputs coupled through softmax create a valid probability distribution over all classes; categorical cross-entropy; mini-batch SGD.

sections.title: Further comparisons and misconceptions
sections.body:
Softmax (one K-way model)One-vs-rest (K sigmoids)
Outputs sum to 1YesNo
Classes mutually exclusiveAssumedNot assumed (multi-label OK)
TrainingJointly, coupledK independent problems
  • "The 0.5 threshold is fixed." It's a choice; move it to trade precision for recall (ROC/PR curves).
  • "Softmax probabilities are calibrated confidences." Often over-confident, especially in deep nets; calibrate with temperature scaling.
  • "High accuracy means a good classifier." Not with imbalanced classes; check per-class recall and macro-F1.
  • "Logistic regression is regression." It's a classifier; "regression" refers to modelling log-odds linearly.

code.title: Logistic regression with SGD: the study-hours example
code.explain: Reproduces the two SGD steps on p.33–34 exactly, shows the progress check, trains for 500 epochs, and recomputes the binary-metrics example and BCE values.
mistakes: Computing log(σ(z)) naively: overflow/log(0) for large |z|; use log-sigmoid.
code.notes: PyTorch: nn.Linear(d, 1) with nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss (fuses sigmoid + BCE stably).
code.code:
# Logistic regression as one sigmoid neuron trained with SGD: the session's study-hours example (NumPy)
import numpy as np
np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True)
sigmoid = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
X = np.array([[1, 1], [1, 2], [1, 3], [1, 4]], float)   # bias column + hours studied
y = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1], float)                        # pass?
bce = lambda w: -np.mean(y * np.log(sigmoid(X @ w)) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - sigmoid(X @ w)))
w = np.zeros(2); eta = 0.5
print(f"w0 = {w}, predictions {sigmoid(X @ w)}, loss {bce(w):.4f}")
for i in (0, 2):                                        # the slides' two SGD steps: example 1, then example 3
    p = sigmoid(X[i] @ w); g = (p - y[i]) * X[i]          # eq. (10)
    w = w - eta * g
    print(f"SGD on example {i+1}: z = {X[i] @ w + eta * g @ X[i]:.3f}  y_hat = {p:.3f}  error = {p - y[i]:.3f}  grad = {g}  w = {w}")
p2 = sigmoid(X @ w)
print("predictions after 2 steps:", p2, " loss", round(bce(w), 4))
print("examples 1-2 (label 0) moved from 0.5 to", p2[:2], "-> away from 0 after these two updates")
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for epoch in range(1, 501):                             # keep going: shuffled SGD epochs
    for i in rng.permutation(4):
        w -= eta * (sigmoid(X[i] @ w) - y[i]) * X[i]
    if epoch in (1, 10, 100, 500): print(f"epoch {epoch:3d}: w = {w}  loss = {bce(w):.4f}  preds = {sigmoid(X @ w)}")
print("decision boundary (hours where p = 0.5): x =", round(-w[0] / w[1], 3))
# BCE values from the slides' intuition
for yh in (0.9, 0.5, 0.1, 0.01): print(f"y=1, y_hat={yh}: loss = {-np.log(yh):.3f}")
# binary metrics example (p.43)
t = np.array([1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0]); p = np.array([1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0])
TP = int(((t == 1) & (p == 1)).sum()); TN = int(((t == 0) & (p == 0)).sum()); FP = int(((t == 0) & (p == 1)).sum()); FN = int(((t == 1) & (p == 0)).sum())
P, R = TP / (TP + FP), TP / (TP + FN)
print(f"TP={TP} TN={TN} FP={FP} FN={FN}  accuracy={(TP+TN)/8}  precision={P}  recall={R}  F1={2*P*R/(P+R)}")

code.title: Softmax regression with mini-batches, inference and metrics
code.explain: Stable softmax, the p.73–78 mini-batch step (with corrected values), training to convergence, the inference example, categorical CE values, the multi-class confusion-matrix metrics and top-k.
mistakes: Applying softmax then nn.CrossEntropyLoss (which applies log-softmax again).
Normalising over the batch axis instead of the class axis.
code.notes: PyTorch: nn.Linear(d, K) + nn.CrossEntropyLoss on raw logits with integer labels; DataLoader(shuffle=True, batch_size=128).
code.code:
# Softmax regression: the session's mini-batch example, inference and multi-class metrics (NumPy)
import numpy as np
np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True)
def softmax(Z):
    Z = Z - Z.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True)                # stable softmax (translation invariance)
    E = np.exp(Z); return E / E.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
print("softmax([2, 1, 0.1]) =", softmax(np.array([2.0, 1.0, 0.1])))
X = np.array([[1, 1, 2], [1, 2, 1], [1, 2, 3], [1, 3, 2]], float)   # bias, x1, x2
labels = np.array([1, 2, 1, 3]); Y = np.eye(3)[labels - 1]          # one-hot
W = np.array([[0.1, -0.1, 0.2], [0.2, 0.1, -0.1], [-0.1, 0.2, 0.1]])
XB, YB = X[:2], Y[:2]; eta = 0.1; B = 2
Z = XB @ W; P = softmax(Z)
print("Z_B =\n", Z); print("Y_hat_B =\n", P)
G = XB.T @ (P - YB) / B                                  # eq. (25)
print("grad =\n", G); W1 = W - eta * G; print("W1 =\n", W1)
cce = lambda W, Xs, Ys: -np.mean(np.sum(Ys * np.log(softmax(Xs @ W)), axis=1))
print(f"mini-batch loss before {cce(W, XB, YB):.4f} after {cce(W1, XB, YB):.4f}")
# keep training: mini-batch SGD with shuffling
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); W = W.copy()
for epoch in range(1, 2001):
    idx = rng.permutation(4)
    for s in range(0, 4, B):
        b = idx[s:s + B]; W -= 0.5 * X[b].T @ (softmax(X[b] @ W) - Y[b]) / B
    if epoch in (1, 100, 2000): print(f"epoch {epoch}: loss {cce(W, X, Y):.4f}  predicted classes {softmax(X @ W).argmax(1) + 1}")
# inference example (p.82): logits given directly
z = np.array([1.2, 2.5, 0.8]); p = softmax(z); print("inference: y_hat =", p, " class", p.argmax() + 1)
# categorical cross-entropy intuition table (p.62)
for q in (0.8, 0.5, 0.2, 0.05): print(f"p(true class) = {q}: loss = {-np.log(q):.2f}")
# multi-class confusion matrix (p.85)
C = np.array([[45, 3, 2], [5, 38, 7], [2, 4, 44]])
prec = np.diag(C) / C.sum(0); rec = np.diag(C) / C.sum(1); f1 = 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec)
print("accuracy", round(np.trace(C) / C.sum(), 4)); print("precision", prec, "recall", rec, "F1", f1)
w = C.sum(1) / C.sum(); print(f"macro precision {prec.mean():.3f}, weighted precision {(w * prec).sum():.3f}, macro F1 {f1.mean():.3f}")
# top-k accuracy
S = rng.normal(size=(1000, 10)); t = rng.integers(0, 10, 1000)
top5 = np.argsort(-S, 1)[:, :5]; print("random scores: top-1", (S.argmax(1) == t).mean(), " top-5", np.mean([t[i] in top5[i] for i in range(1000)]))
print("iterations per epoch for N=60000, B=128:", int(np.ceil(60000 / 128)))
